content: When there are multiple types of interventions available for the same indication, it is essential to provide evidence to support decision-making by health programs. Advocacy for fair pricing of drugs, such as rifapentine, is necessary to facilitate the widespread implementation of new recommendations. Kerri Viney from the WHO Global TB Programme began her presentation by sharing the latest epidemiological data on the burden of tuberculosis (TB) in children and adolescents. She emphasized the significant challenges in detecting TB cases and ensuring access to tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) for these age groups. The differential impact of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic on children compared to adults was also discussed. She reviewed the most recent updates to WHO guidance on managing TB in children and adolescents, which followed a meeting of the WHO-convened Guideline Development Group in May-June 2021. New recommendations and associated research gaps highlighted in the WHO Rapid Communication on TB management in children and adolescents were presented. Updated consolidated guidelines and an operational handbook containing detailed information on these new recommendations and implementation guidance will be published by WHO in the coming weeks. Ongoing studies that may inform future policy updates were also discussed. The Chair opened the floor for discussion, focusing on the following questions: 1. Are there additional critical evidence gaps or upcoming studies that need to be addressed? 2. What strategies should WHO/GTB employ to encourage investment in pediatric TB research and development and to shorten research timelines to improve global TB care policies? 3. What strategies should WHO/GTB use to enhance the implementation and evaluation of global TB policy guidance for children and adolescents? During the discussion: On screening and diagnosis, it was noted that optimizing the diagnostic yield from respiratory and non-respiratory samples in children is crucial for accurate diagnosis of both drug-susceptible (DS-TB) and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). Evaluation of computer-aided detection software tailored to pediatric disease patterns is also needed to assess its utility in young children. On prevention, the lack of data on the optimal daily dosage of rifapentine for young children remains a challenge. On treatment, translating the new recommendation for a 4-month regimen to treat children with non-severe DS-TB into practice is critical. However, countries will require support in defining non-severe TB in children, scaling up access to chest radiography, and building capacity through training. Additionally, the lack of age-appropriate formulations poses a disproportionate challenge in treating DR-TB. On implementation and access, optimizing care models is essential to improve case detection and TPT uptake. Addressing barriers to healthcare access, such as household literacy and contact screening strategies, may enable earlier access to care. Developing composite indicators to monitor progress in child and adolescent TB at national and sub-national levels could accelerate efforts toward achieving the targets of the UN High-Level Meeting on Ending TB. Better estimation of the TB burden in children and adolescents can promote the scaling up of tailored interventions. Regarding future research, the inclusion of children and adolescents in clinical trials across diverse geographic settings is critical to ensure the generalizability of findings. Operationalizing this requires resolving confusion around the definition of children and adolescents, which could be based on clinical disease spectrum rather than age cutoffs used for surveillance and reporting. The impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on TB development in children and adolescents warrants further study. Kerri Viney also presented on TB comorbidities and vulnerable populations, identifying priority drivers for TB and risk factors for poor treatment outcomes, including alcohol use disorders, diabetes, HIV infection, malnutrition, smoking, and mental health issues. Member states have committed to strengthening integrated care for TB and these comorbidities through respective UN High-Level Meeting political declarations. However, despite existing WHO guidelines, countries have been slow to scale up action to address TB comorbidities, except for HIV-associated TB. To address this, WHO/GTB is developing a Framework for Collaborative Action on TB and Comorbidities, building on the experience of the WHO Policy on Collaborative TB/HIV Activities. This framework aims to establish and strengthen collaboration across health programs and sectors to deliver people-centered services for individuals with TB and comorbidities. Ongoing studies that may shape policies on co-management of TB and comorbidities were presented. The Chair opened the floor for discussion, focusing on: 1. Awareness of new evidence that could influence recommendations on TB and diabetes, TB and undernutrition, and TB and HIV. 2. Further guidance or updates needed to enhance the implementation of global TB policy guidance for people with TB and comorbidities and vulnerable populations. 3. Support required to accelerate the translation of global TB policy guidance into practice. Participants welcomed WHO/GTB’s plans to consolidate recommendations and guidelines on TB and comorbidities and develop the Framework for Collaborative Action on TB and Comorbidities, emphasizing person-centered care. The ongoing evidence review on TB and hepatitis B/C co-infection was acknowledged as a significant advancement. Including individuals with comorbidities in TB research across all age groups is essential to address evidence gaps, particularly for conditions with limited data, such as co-management of alcohol and tobacco dependence. Developing standardized study protocols with clear definitions of relevant sub-populations and endpoints can help generate high-quality evidence for policy. On implementation, the development of an operational handbook on TB and comorbidities must address logistical challenges, such as managing drug-drug interactions and toxicities at the primary healthcare level. A multisectoral approach, including joint programming across health programs and other sectors, is crucial to address the broader determinants of TB comorbidities and TB in vulnerable populations. Lessons from joint programming in TB/HIV and efforts to co-manage TB and COVID-19 can inform scaling up collaborative action on TB and comorbidities. Mapping TB vulnerability at national and sub-national levels can support prioritization and implementation of relevant actions. Ernesto Jaramillo presented on TB social protection and associated disability, emphasizing the need for person-centered TB care and prevention services within the broader context of universal health coverage and multisectoral action. Current WHO guidance on social protection and patient support for TB was discussed, along with ways to strengthen these approaches in line with the End TB Strategy goals. Research gaps on TB and social protection were highlighted, and WHO/GTB’s plans to repackage existing recommendations into a TB social protection guidance and develop policy guidance on managing TB-associated disability were shared. Participants discussed missing policy areas in TB social protection, effective approaches to address challenges in current policy, and strategies to develop evidence for TB-associated disability policies. Suggestions included developing indicators to measure progress in social protection coverage, compiling case studies of best practices, and conducting cost-effectiveness studies. Evidence is needed to better characterize individuals at risk of TB-associated disabilities, the determinants, types of care required, and outcomes post-TB treatment. Randomized trials and other studies are necessary to build high-quality evidence for policy and expand understanding of predictors of chronic disease post-TB. Dennis Falzon presented on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on TB services, addressing common questions on co-management of TB and COVID-19 and describing WHO/GTB’s efforts to support national TB programs during the pandemic. This includes monitoring the impact of the COVID-19 response on TB notifications, issuing guidance on maintaining TB services during the pandemic, and sharing case studies of programmatic innovations. An ongoing review of evidence on the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and TB disease with unfavorable treatment outcomes was also presented. Participants welcomed WHO/GTB’s actions on TB and COVID-19 and discussed the need for guidance on preventing drug-drug interactions between Paxlovid and rifamycinor bedaquiline-containing TB regimens. In conclusion, participants emphasized the importance of prioritizing policy-relevant research gaps and supporting their implementation. Research should include individuals of all age groups and vulnerabilities, considering the acceptability, feasibility, and equity impacts of interventions. WHO was encouraged to advocate for research implementation to strengthen recommendations where evidence certainty is low. In the interim, generalized evidence synthesis using trial and non-trial data may address evidence gaps. Participants highlighted the value of infographics to simplify guideline presentations and knowledge-sharing platforms. WHO reaffirmed its commitment to convening regular forums to share policy development plans.
